name: Shun (peak-flavour season)
text: The period when an ingredient tastes best and is most plentiful; Japanese dictionaries gloss it as the time of fullest flavour and abundant supply. In kitchen usage it is the umbrella term, subdivided into hashiri (first), sakari (peak) and nagori (last) stages.
flavor: Heard on menus and at markets: 'this is shun now'.
use: 'Kono sakana wa ima ga shun desu.' Used to justify a menu choice, a price, or a cooking method matched to the ingredient's condition.
craft: Shun is not a single point: the sources split it into three stages, and one cited article stresses that the sakari stage is not automatically the best, since taste and texture shift through the season. Chefs choose the stage, not just the month.
src: Ryori Kagaku no Mori: three stages of shun

name: Hashiri (the first run of the season)
text: The first stage of an ingredient's season, when it has just begun to appear. Hashiri items are treated as hatsumono (first-of-year produce), draw attention and are often traded at high prices. Eating them was regarded as stylish (iki).
flavor: Said with anticipation and a hint of luxury: 'hashiri no takenoko'.
use: Menu notes such as 'hashiri no ayu' or 'hashiri no shin-cha' signal the earliest, scarce appearance of the item.
craft: You pay for novelty and scarcity at this stage; the sources describe it as valued for the 'first' encounter rather than for peak abundance. Judge whether the guest is buying the season's arrival or the ingredient's best condition.
src: Ryori Kagaku no Mori: three stages of shun

name: Sakari (the peak of the season)
text: The middle stage of an ingredient's season, when it is at its fullest ripeness and most abundant. Because large volumes reach the market, prices are generally lower than during hashiri.
flavor: Used for 'right now, plenty of it, good price'.
use: 'Ima ga sakari' at a market stall; a menu built around a sakari ingredient is easier to cost and to supply.
craft: The sources note a caution: peak abundance is not always peak flavour, since one ingredient changes in taste and texture across the season. Check the individual lot rather than relying on the calendar.
src: Ryori Kagaku no Mori: three stages of shun

name: Nagori (the lingering end of the season)
text: The closing stage of an ingredient's season, with a sense of bidding farewell to the season and looking to next year's return. Sources note that in this stage moisture tends to fall and fibres firm up, though depth and richness (koku) can be enjoyed.
flavor: Wistful, poetic: 'nagori no ...' on late-season menus.
use: 'Nagori no sanma', 'nagori no hamo'. Served with a note that this is the last of the year.
craft: Because moisture drops and fibre hardens, the sources suggest cooking that restores moisture, such as simmering or steaming. Do not treat nagori as a defect; it is a deliberate, sentimental menu category.
src: Ryori Kagaku no Mori: three stages of shun
Eco-chil: hashiri, sakari, nagori of vegetables

name: Hatsumono (first-of-the-year produce)
text: The first fish, vegetables, fruit or grain taken in a given year in its season. An Edo-period saying, hatsumono shichijugo-nichi, held that eating hatsumono lengthens life by 75 days. Today shincha, soba and shinmai are still treated as hatsumono.
use: 'Hatsumono desu' on a plate presented early in the season; the saying is quoted when serving the first of an item.
craft: The appeal is auspiciousness and novelty rather than quality; the first lots are priced for that. The 75-day belief is a folk saying, not a measured claim.

name: Hatsu-gatsuo (first bonito of the year)
text: Bonito riding the Kuroshio north along the Pacific coast in spring to early summer, around May. Katsuo was also written 'winning fish' (勝魚), a lucky charm for contests. The Edo shogunate's 1665 (Kanbun 5) schedule for fish, birds and vegetables set April (May in the modern calendar) as the start of its appearance.
flavor: Lean, clean-tasting; symbol of early summer.
use: Served as tataki or sashimi in May. Tokyo's market authority lists it under seasonal fish.
craft: Hatsu-gatsuo is lighter and leaner than the fatter modori-gatsuo of autumn; do not judge it by fat. Its price reflects Edo-era hatsumono fever more than richness.
src: Tokyo Metropolitan Central Wholesale Market: hatsu-gatsuo

name: Modori-gatsuo (returning bonito of autumn)
text: Bonito heading south again in autumn, after the spring northward run that produces hatsu-gatsuo. Sources describe it as fatty, in contrast to the lighter hatsu-gatsuo.
use: Contrasted with hatsu-gatsuo on menus: 'hatsu' in spring, 'modori' in autumn.
craft: Pair seasoning to fat level: stronger garnish and seasoning suit the fatty autumn fish, restrained ones suit the lean spring fish. Know which run your lot belongs to before choosing the preparation.
src: Yaizu Yamafuku: Edo power food hatsu-gatsuo
Tsuri News: hatsu-gatsuo and Edo hatsumono taste

name: Shincha and Hachijuhachiya (new tea; the 88th night)
text: Shincha is the first tea of the year. Hachijuhachiya, the 88th night counted from Risshun (start of spring), is the traditional marker; tea harvested then is regarded as auspicious. One source links shinmai to the number 88 in the same way.
use: 'Shincha' labels on tea in spring; 'hachijuhachiya no cha' for tea tied to the date.
craft: The date is a calendar count from Risshun, not a quality grade; the term signals timing and good luck. Check actual harvest date and lot, not the label alone.

name: Shinmai (new-crop rice)
text: Rice of the current year's harvest, treated as a hatsumono in autumn along with shincha and soba. Harvested paddy is dried to roughly 15 percent moisture, then hulled (momisuri) into brown rice.
flavor: Fresh, fragrant, moist; the autumn headline.
use: 'Shinmai' labelling on packs and menus from early autumn.
craft: New-crop rice carries more moisture than rice stored through the year, so water ratios and soaking habits are normally reviewed at changeover; this is a cooking-practice nuance rather than a figure from the cited sources.

name: Inekari (rice harvesting)
text: Cutting the ripened rice plant, normally at the base. Cutting only the ears is called hokubigari or hokari. Autumn festivals (aki-matsuri) celebrate a safe harvest and pray for a good crop next year.
flavor: The start of the rice year.
use: 'Inekari no jiki' in a farm calendar; harvest timing drives shinmai arrival dates.
craft: Harvest method decides downstream steps: hung and sun-dried (hasakake) or machine-dried. Ask which a farm uses when judging a rice's description.
src: Colocal: rice making, harvest and hasakake

name: Hasakake (hanging harvested rice to dry)
text: Hanging bundled rice on poles or racks to dry in sun and natural wind for about two weeks. Regional names include inekake and toka. Because it is laborious compared with machine drying, today it is mostly seen in hilly or upland areas where machinery is hard to use.
flavor: Traditional, labour-intensive; a selling point on premium rice.
use: 'Hasakake-mai' or 'tenpi-boshi' on packaging means sun-dried rice.
craft: Sources give drying to about 15 percent moisture as the target. The phrase is a process claim: ask about location and duration, since hanging time and weather vary.
src: Colocal: rice making, harvest and hasakake

name: Momisuri (hulling paddy to brown rice)
text: Removing the hull (momigara) from paddy (momi) to produce brown rice (genmai). It follows threshing and drying in the harvest sequence.
use: 'Momisuri-go no genmai' on farm lot specifications.
craft: Hulling gives brown rice; polishing to white rice is a later, separate step. Keep the two stages distinct when reading specifications.
src: Nochi: full rice harvest work explained

name: Hatsuho (first ears offered to the gods)
text: A harvest rite in which a few ears are pulled before the actual harvest and offered to the gods; an Ehime folklore record also mentions offering roasted new rice. It is a form of offering the first of the crop to the divine.
use: Heard in shrine and farm-festival contexts; 'hatsuho' also appears in shrine offering terminology.
craft: It shows the same logic as hatsumono: the first of the harvest belongs to the gods before people. Do not conflate with commercial shinmai sales.

name: Nijushi sekki (the 24 solar terms)
text: A calendar dividing the year into 24 parts on the basis of the sun's movement, used historically as a guide for farm work. Seasonal markers such as Risshun (start of spring) and Shubun (autumn equinox) belong to it.
flavor: Calendar-poetic; used on seasonal menus and wagashi names.
use: Menus and tea-ceremony sweets are titled by sekki; 'Risshun' marks the count to hachijuhachiya.
craft: Sekki are astronomical dates that move slightly each year, and they are not the same as weather; Japanese climate lags the calendar, so food choices follow actual supply.
src: Yahoo Weather: enjoying seasons by shichijuniko

name: Shichijuni-ko (the 72 micro-seasons)
text: Each of the 24 sekki is divided into three, about five days each, giving 72 periods, each named for weather or the state of plants and animals. Examples: seri-sunawachi-sakau (Shokan, parsley blooms), takenoko-shozu (Rikka, bamboo shoots appear), mizu-hajimete-karuru (late Shubun), linked to mukago rice.
use: Seasonal kaiseki titles and menu notes often cite the current ko.
craft: The names describe observed nature, not guaranteed supply. Use the ko as a seasonal prompt and verify actual availability of seri, takenoko or mukago.
src: Yahoo Weather: enjoying seasons by shichijuniko
Chugokugo-script: meaning and history of shichijuniko

name: Gyoji-shoku (festival and event foods)
text: Special dishes eaten at seasonal events and celebrations. The Ministry of Agriculture (MAFF) frames them as carrying wishes for the family's happiness and health.
use: Used in shokuiku (food education), department-store seasonal displays, and menus pegged to events.
craft: Meanings (puns, shapes, auspiciousness) are traditional associations, and origins are often disputed. Quote one source's explanation as 'one account' rather than fact when stories differ.

name: Osechi (New Year dishes)
text: New Year festival food. MAFF explains symbolic items: kuromame (black soybeans) so the family stays mame (healthy, diligent), kazunoko (herring roe) for descendants prospering from many eggs, and kuri-kinton (chestnut paste) for wealth.
use: Gifted or ordered as multi-tiered boxes; each item is introduced by its meaning.
craft: Meanings rest on wordplay and symbolism. Use MAFF's wording when explaining items to guests, and keep to what the ministry states.
src: Happy Tasty: osechi and sekku dishes

name: Setsubun and ehomaki (bean-throwing and lucky-direction roll)
text: Setsubun foods: beans, believed to have power to drive off evil, and the ehomaki nori roll eaten facing the lucky direction. Origins of ehomaki are disputed; the leading theory places it in Osaka, among merchants hoping for prosperity, sometimes described as originating in the Edo to Meiji-era Osaka pleasure quarters.
use: Seasonal sushi counters and convenience stores in early February.
craft: Treat the Osaka-origin story as the leading theory, not settled fact. Sources vary on era and setting.

name: Tanabata somen (somen for the Star Festival)
text: Somen is the representative Tanabata event food. Origins vary: one explanation likens the noodles to the threads Orihime weaves, another to the Milky Way.
use: Served chilled on or near 7 July.
craft: Both explanations are folk interpretations. Say 'one account holds' when presenting them.

name: Nanakusa-gayu (seven-herb rice porridge)
text: Porridge with seven spring herbs eaten on 7 January. An account in the search results says it combined a custom from China with the native practice of picking young greens (wakana-tsumi). Seri (parsley) is one of the seven herbs.
use: Eaten in the first week of the year.
craft: The synthesis of Chinese custom and local wakana-picking is a common explanation; the exact seven herbs are not enumerated in the sources cited here.

name: Naorai (post-ritual shared meal and sake)
text: After a shrine ritual, the offered food and sake (omiki) are consumed by priests and participants. Jinja Honcho explains the core meaning as shared eating of the gods' offerings, which unites gods and people. Today it is often simplified to drinking omiki, and in popular understanding it is the banquet after a ritual.
flavor: Warm, communal; said at shrine events.
use: 'Naorai ni sanka suru' after a festival or ceremony.
craft: Wikipedia warns that reading naorai simply as 'ending abstinence' (gesai) is incomplete. Etymology is debated (naori-ai, or return to normal). It is more than a party.

name: Shinjin-kyoshoku (gods and people eating together)
text: The idea that sharing offered food joins people and gods and brings the gods' blessing (mitama no fuyu). Jinja Honcho gives it as the root meaning of naorai. It gives the court's Niiname-sai as an example, in which the Emperor offers new grain to the gods and eats it himself.
use: Explains why offerings are eaten, not discarded.
craft: Underlies the Japanese custom of drinking sacred sake at festivals; the sacred is meant to be consumed, not only displayed.

name: Ichiju-sansai (one soup, three sides)
text: A menu structure of one soup and three side dishes (one main plus two sides), counted alongside rice. Its roots are in honzen ryori; in that tradition the three are namasu, a simmered dish and a grilled dish, and pickles (kō no mono) are not counted.
use: Used in nutrition guidance and in assembling set meals.
craft: The count excludes rice and pickles. Some explanations say Zen temples of the Kamakura era normally served ichiju-issai, with ichiju-sansai on special days.
src: Olive Hitomawashi: basics and history of ichiju-sansai

name: Honzen ryori (formal tray banquet cuisine)
text: A formal banquet cuisine of samurai society that took shape in the Muromachi period. Formats include ichiju-sansai, ni-ju go-sai and san-ju shichi-sai; the dictionary entry gives ni-ju go-sai (two soups, five sides) as the usual form.
use: Reference for formal service structure and for the origin of ichiju-sansai.
craft: Kaiseki later inherited the form according to some accounts, so honzen is the ancestor of the soup-plus-sides count.
src: Olive Hitomawashi: basics and history of ichiju-sansai

name: Umami (the fifth basic taste)
text: One of the five basic tastes, with sweet, sour, salty and bitter, associated with dashi. Kikunae Ikeda of Tokyo Imperial University identified it in kombu dashi in 1908; glutamate itself was found by Ritthausen in 1866. Ikeda's patent was filed 24 April 1908 and registered 25 July 1908.
flavor: Savoury depth; the word chefs use for dashi.
use: 'Umami' is used internationally; Japanese professionals specify the source (kombu, katsuobushi, shiitake).
craft: Ikeda's contribution was tracing the taste to glutamate, not discovering the compound. The search found no source on kokumi, so it is not covered here.
src: National Diet Library: discovery of umami

name: Fudo and GI (place character and geographical indication)
text: Fudo is the climate, natural and human conditions of a place. Japan's Geographical Indication (GI) system registers names of products whose quality and reputation are tied to such a place. The GI law was passed in June 2014 and took effect the following June.
use: GI mark on registered products.
craft: Japanese official texts use fudo, climate and regional character rather than the loan word terroir. Registration covers production area and method as well as the name.

name: Kinryoki and kaikin (closed season and its opening)
text: Kinryoki is a period when fishing is banned to protect resources, set often around spawning. The day after it ends is the kaikin (opening) day. For ayu, kaikin falls around 1 June, varying by region.
use: 'Kaikin-bi' announcements for ayu, crab and others.
craft: Opening dates are set by region and species; check the current year's notice. Opening day often carries first-catch price premiums.

name: Ryoki (fishing season)
text: The legal or customary period in which a species may be fished. For matsubagani, the season runs from the 6 November opening to about 20 March, roughly five months. Female zuwai-gani is basically fished only to the end of December per one source.
use: Ordering windows with crab suppliers follow the ryoki.
craft: Sex, species and sea area change the season; confirm against the supplier's current-year notice.

name: Matsubagani (male snow crab, opening 6 November)
text: Trade name for male zuwai-gani landed in the San'in region (Tottori Sakai is one cited landing). Sources state the opening day is 6 November in all matsubagani waters, set by ministry ordinance by sea area, and the season lasts to about 20 March. Beni-zuwai (red snow crab) opens earlier, on 1 September.
use: Orders are heavy right after 6 November; advance booking is advised.
craft: A brand name for male crab in a given region; check the sea area and the current-year notice.
